claims.text: A machine-learning-accelerated two-phase coexistence simulation can reproduce the melting temperature of refractory materials.
The method can reproduce the entropy and enthalpy of fusion and the volume change at melting.
The method has accuracy comparable to a full ab initio free-energy approach.
Using machine-learning potentials significantly reduces computational cost relative to thermodynamic integration with AIMD.
Machine-learning potentials calibrated to DFT data can replace full thermodynamic integration with AIMD in the proposed framework.
Appropriate boundary conditions can sustain solid-liquid interfaces in dynamic equilibrium near the melting temperature.
Machine-learning potentials can accurately emulate DFT-calculated interatomic interactions in both solid and liquid phases.
Direct observation of solid-liquid coexistence allows extraction of the melting point.
Latent heat obtained from the simulation permits calculation of the entropy and enthalpy of fusion.
Changes in simulation-cell volume can be used to determine the volume change at melting.
The proposed method is expected to be reliable for refractory materials with moderate anharmonic effects.
Systems with extreme anharmonicity or very complex phase behavior may require additional validation.
The error relative to full AIMD thermodynamic integration may depend on the material and simulation parameters.

contradictions.description: The hypothesis and mechanism specify a two-phase coexistence simulation with an explicit solid-liquid interface, whereas the intervention treats a two-phase method and the Z method as interchangeable alternatives. The Z method is not itself an explicit two-phase coexistence framework, so the stated coexistence-based mechanism does not consistently apply to both alternatives.
